title: Maximum Number of Non-Overlapping Substrings
statement:
The string `s` is made of lowercase English letters. Choose non-empty substrings of `s` that obey both rules:

- No two chosen substrings share a position: for any two of them, one ends strictly before the other starts.
- A chosen substring is closed: whenever it contains a letter, it contains every occurrence of that letter in `s`.

Choose as many substrings as possible and return them. If several selections reach that maximum count, return the one whose lengths add up to the least; that selection is always unique. The substrings may be returned in any order.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Call a substring closed when it holds every copy of each letter it contains. Two closed substrings can never partly overlap: one lies inside the other or they are apart. A closed substring always starts at some letter's first occurrence, and for each letter there is at most one smallest closed substring starting there, found by stretching its range until it covers every letter inside it. With only 26 letters that gives at most 26 candidates. The best answer keeps the innermost ones: sweep the candidates by start, and when a new one starts inside the last kept one, it is nested in it and replaces it.

## Approach

1. Record `first` and `last`, each letter's first and last index.
2. For every `start` that is the first occurrence of its letter, set `end = last[letter]` and scan `j` from `start` to `end`, extending `end` to cover each letter met.
3. If some letter inside has `first[inner] < start`, no closed substring starts here; skip it.
4. Otherwise `s[start..end]` is closed. If `start > prevEnd` it is disjoint from the last kept piece, so open a new slot; either way, write it into the last slot (replacing a piece that contains it) and set `prevEnd = end`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "adefaddaccc"`. From `start = 0` (`a`), `end` grows to 7 and `"adefadda"` is kept with `prevEnd = 7`. At `start = 1` (`d`) the scan meets the `a` at index 4, whose first copy is at 0, so `d` is skipped. `start = 2` (`e`) gives `"e"`; since 2 is not past 7 it replaces `"adefadda"`, and `prevEnd = 2`. `start = 3` gives `"f"` in a new slot, and `start = 8` gives `"ccc"` in another. The result is `["e", "f", "ccc"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(26 · n): at most 26 candidate starts, each scanning at most n characters.
- Space: O(1) besides the output (two arrays of 26).

## Pitfalls

- A letter's range `[first, last]` is not closed by itself; letters inside can push `end` further right or make it invalid by reaching left.
- Taking the longest or the leftmost pieces loses count: `"ef"` must give way to `"e"` and `"f"`.
- Only first occurrences can start a closed substring; testing every index wastes time and can add wrong pieces.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `first`, `last` | each letter's first and last index (`n` and `-1` when absent) |
| `start`, `end` | the candidate closed substring being built |
| `valid` | whether the candidate stayed closed |
| `prevEnd` | end index of the last kept piece |
| `result` | the kept pieces |

narration.3: first[letter] will hold the letter's first index; n marks a letter that never appears.
narration.4: last[letter] will hold its last index; -1 marks a letter that never appears.
narration.5: One pass over s records where every letter begins and ends.
